blocks.text: Third, for Jonathan תנשמת thinsemeth is סלמנדרא salamandra. And for Erpenius' Arabic translator it is صنبرص [ṣnbrṣ] senabras, a corruption of سامابرص [sāmābrṣ] sammabras, as the Paris edition has it. I think these have come closest to the truth, and that, as with the five preceding names, this name too denotes some species of lizard, namely the chameleon, which is so called from breathing. For in Hebrew נשם is to breathe, and נשמה means not only spirit but also breath or breathing, as does נשימה. Hence, on these words of Psal. CL, 6. כל נשמה תהלל יה, Let every spirit praise God, the author of Bereshit Rabba, ch. 14, says: על כל נשימה ונשימה שאדם נישם צריך לקלס לבוראו מה טעם כל נשמה תהלל יה כל הנשימה תהלל יה For every breath that a man breathes he must praise his Creator. For what reason? (Because it is said) „Let every spirit praise the Lord“, that is, Let every breath praise the Lord. Anyone who has a clear understanding of its nature must admit that the chameleon is rightly named from breathing, or from breathing in: for since it keeps its mouth open in a perpetual gape and draws in air with its breath, many believe that it feeds on air alone. Pliny, book 8, chapter 33: It holds itself erect, with its mouth always open, and alone of animals is nourished neither by food nor by drink, nor by any nourishment other than air. Solinus: Its gaping is perpetual and serves no use; for it takes no food, is not nourished by drink, and lives on no other nourishment than the air it draws in. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15:
That too, the animal that is fed on winds and air.
